entries.title: Why the kill gate doesn't fire
entries.summary: A committee can have the power to stop a failing program and still approve more funding. People who approved it may want to keep it going. For a big program, let someone with no prior approval decide after a missed target.
entries.metaDescription: A kill gate often fails because the continue-or-stop decision goes back to the people who approved the program. Let a reviewer who did not approve it decide.
entries.operatingMove: For a big program, record its minimum result, due date, how the sponsor will be judged, and a reviewer who did not approve it.
entries.preview: A committee can have the power to stop a program and still extend it. Research suggests that people may add money to an earlier choice after it goes badly. For a big or hard-to-reverse program, set a minimum at approval. Judge sponsors on the case. If the program falls short, a reviewer who did not approve it decides.
entries.bodyHtml:
A program is late and costing more than planned. The sponsor asks for one more quarter. The committee that approved the first funding rounds can stop the work, but it approves the request. A quarter later, the same choice returns.

A tougher gate will not solve that problem by itself. The committee already had the power to stop. The people deciding also helped make the commitment they now have to end.

Studies of escalation show that people who own a losing choice often keep putting resources into it. A long-running review found the pull was stronger in four samples when authority was shared. A funding review puts a sponsor before the committee that approved the same case.

The answer is not to remove the sponsor. The sponsor knows the work. Move only the continue-or-stop decision after a pre-set miss.

First, record the minimum result and its due date. It is the point below which the original case no longer holds. It is not the forecast.

Second, tell the sponsor that the review will judge the quality of the case and how early a miss is raised. Do not judge only the final result.

Third, name a reviewer who had no part in the approval. When the minimum is missed, the sponsor brings the evidence and recommends continue, narrow, pause, or stop. The reviewer decides. The EPMO tracks the date and calls the review.

The reviewer can still continue a program on a revised case. Use this step for large or hard-to-reverse commitments. The evidence comes from laboratory studies, a small shared-authority sample, and related field studies; no study has tested this full design.

At the next funding approval, write the minimum, its date, how the sponsor will be judged, and who decides after a miss. The next request for one more quarter then goes to someone who does not have to reverse an earlier approval.

entries.title: Who owns governance?
entries.summary: In a meeting that crosses domains, every domain signs off on its own area. Nobody in the room owns the enterprise decision itself. A stack of approvals is not a decision — so who owns it?
entries.metaDescription: Every domain signs off on its own area and nobody owns the enterprise decision. Six questions an EPMO answers to turn a stack of approvals into one choice.
entries.operatingMove: For any decision big enough to cross domains, have the EPMO answer six questions before approval. What outcome are we after, and who owns it? Which rules and limits apply? What do we know about conditions now? What options are still open, and what does each cost the portfolio? Who decides, and who can grant an exception? What would reopen the decision?
entries.preview: The sponsor asks whether the program is approved to proceed. Security, data governance, architecture, operations, and finance each give a defensible answer. Together they describe an investment nobody actually chose. This field note shows why a stack of approvals leaves the enterprise decision unmade, and which part of governance the EPMO should own.
entries.bodyHtml:
The sponsor asks one question: "Are we approved to proceed?"

Security says yes, as long as the rollout is more tightly controlled. Data governance says yes, but not using customer transcripts the way the plan assumes. Architecture can support the design once one dependency is cleared. Operations can't run the old and new processes side by side for the whole switchover. Finance points out that all of these changes remove the cheaper option and push the payoff date back.

Every team is right about its own area. Add the answers up, though, and you get an investment nobody actually chose. All those approvals put the decision on the table. None of them made it.

The missing job

Think about driving. The road authority sets the rules. The car has its limits and safety systems. The driver picks the destination and owns the trip. Navigation pulls the destination, the traffic, the closures, and the routes into one view so the driver can choose. It doesn't write the traffic laws, and it doesn't decide where to go. It just makes a responsible choice possible.

That navigation role is the one missing in the meeting, and it's the one the EPMO should own: the framework around a cross-domain choice. What is being decided, which evidence has to be weighed, what options remain, and who has the authority to decide.

Approvals are not a decision

A strategic program can finish every review and still be ungoverned. Each condition can be sound on its own while, together, they add up to a different investment than the one the sponsor asked the organization to approve. Collecting approvals does not make the decision.

In the meeting above, the plan that was approved no longer works under what's now known. The organization could keep the outcome by funding the tighter design, or narrow the outcome to fit the limits. It could change the order, free up capacity elsewhere, wait, or stop. No single function can make that enterprise choice.

The EPMO shouldn't overrule the specialists. It should show the sponsor whether the original outcome still holds and how the remaining options would affect the portfolio. The record also has to say who can decide and what new evidence would force another look.

What the EPMO owns

Enterprise leaders own the strategic and risk boundaries. Domain leaders own their standards, evidence, and expert judgments. The sponsor owns the outcome. A delegated forum or executive owns the investment decision within its authority. Independent assurance owns its review and challenge.

The EPMO owns the framework that ties the decision together. It keeps track of who owns what and what evidence each domain has to bring. It frames the portfolio options and names who decides and who can grant an exception. It keeps the escalation path, the decision record, and the review triggers. The framework makes sure the authorized decision weighs the right evidence and can be reconstructed later. It doesn't take over the expert judgments or the business outcome.

The framework comes down to six questions. What outcome are we after? Which rules and limits apply? What do we know about current conditions? What options are still open? Who decides, and who can grant an exception? What would reopen the decision? Each one produces something an authorized leader can actually use. Together, they turn separate domain reviews into one enterprise choice without stripping the domains of their authority.

The conversation to have first

When an organization says the EPMO owns governance, start by asking which decisions it means. Assign each standard to its domain owner and the outcome to its sponsor. Name the authority that can accept an exception or change the investment. Then define the evidence that would force another look. Those answers turn a vague assignment into a usable operating model.

The real test is whether a skeptical executive can reconstruct the decision. That executive should be able to see the intended outcome, the limits that applied, and what the experts found. The record should show the options, who decided, the conditions they accepted, and the review trigger. A stack of meetings and status colors can't provide that.

Come back to the sponsor's question. The honest answer isn't a pile of domain approvals. It's the recorded decision an authorized leader made after seeing the conditions and their combined effect on the investment. The framework that makes that decision possible is the part of governance the EPMO owns.

entries.title: Felt productivity is not measured productivity
entries.summary: People can badly misjudge how much AI speeds them up. Judge the tool on what it delivered, measured against a baseline taken before the tool arrived, and keep self-reported speed in a record of its own.
entries.metaDescription: People can badly misjudge how much AI speeds them up. Judge AI adoption on delivered output against a pre-tool baseline, not on self-reported speed.
entries.operatingMove: Before scaling an AI-assisted workflow, require three things: a baseline from before the tool, an output measure that heavier tool use cannot inflate, and a review that keeps felt speed and delivered output in separate columns.
entries.preview: Ask people how much faster AI made them and you get a confident number. It turns out to be a feeling, not evidence. This field note sets a small measurement standard: a baseline captured before the tool arrives, an output measure that heavier tool use cannot inflate, and a review that reads felt speed and delivered output as two separate records. The point is to judge AI adoption on what it delivered, not on how fast it felt.
entries.bodyHtml:
Ask people how much faster AI made them. The answer is almost always a confident number. That number is a feeling, and a feeling is not operating evidence. When a program is funded, scaled, or defended on a self-reported speedup, the organization has let a feeling stand in for evidence.

The finding that should unsettle that habit is not that AI is slow. In a 2025 randomized controlled trial, the research nonprofit METR had sixteen experienced open-source developers complete 246 real tasks, with and without AI. Beforehand they expected a 24 percent speedup. Afterward they still believed they had gained 20 percent. The clock said they took 19 percent longer. The durable lesson is the gap between what capable people believed about their own speed and what the work recorded. That belief survived direct contact with the evidence. The trial does not set a universal effect for every task or tool. It measured expert developers, on codebases they knew well, with early-2025 tools. The gap is the point.

The same split appears across a whole delivery system. Google's DORA program reported in 2024 that teams using AI scored higher on individual productivity, flow, and job satisfaction, while software delivery stability and throughput went down. People felt more productive while the system delivered less stably, in the same dataset. Both findings are snapshots. Together they name the variable a governance standard has to account for. Felt speed and measured output are not the same signal, and the first runs ahead of the second.

People are poor witnesses to their own speed

METR's own February 2026 follow-up is blunt about the self-report problem. Those estimates, it notes, "can be quite unreliable." Wider AI adoption "has made it more difficult to measure task-level productivity," because the comparison against unaided work is eroding. The feeling of fluency — an instant answer, a filled page — is a poor instrument for elapsed time and reworked output. A survey that asks employees how much AI helped is measuring enthusiasm and tool preference, not delivered help.

So the durable claim is not about speed at all. Self-reported speedup is a low-quality signal that systematically runs ahead of measured output. An organization scaling AI on that signal is scaling on sentiment. A portfolio does not fund sentiment on purpose. It does so by default, when no one built the alternative.

What to measure instead

The alternative is ordinary. First, capture a baseline before the tool changes the work. Then choose a work-output signal that reflects delivered value: cycle time, rework, error rate, or finished units meeting standard. Choose it so that using the tool more cannot move it by itself. Finally, review felt experience and delivered outcome in separate columns. When the columns agree, reliance can grow. When they diverge, the review has found the case a satisfaction survey would have counted as a win.

The hard part is deciding which numbers do not count. Adoption rate, active users, prompts per employee, and self-rated speed can all rise while the work stays the same. They belong on an adoption dashboard, not in the evidence a portfolio uses to deepen reliance. A contributed CIO column makes the distinction plainly. Governance machinery can sit above the work, while the value is created or lost inside the workflow. That is why a gain on one task may not reach the result the portfolio funded.

None of this slows adoption. It lets a leader say yes to deeper reliance on evidence, and redirect rather than abandon a tool whose value is leaking inside a workflow. Felt productivity is real and worth having. It is simply not the same thing as measured productivity, and only one of the two can tell a portfolio where its money went.

entries.title: Separate the decision from the outcome
entries.summary: A green target does not prove a good full outcome or a sound approval. Review the outcome, the route, and the first decision separately.
entries.metaDescription: Hitting the funded target does not prove the decision was sound. How to grade decision quality and the full outcome separately in a portfolio review.
entries.operatingMove: At the next review, first grade the decision from its approval record. Then score the full outcome and compare the route taken with the approved route.
entries.preview: A good result can follow a weak decision. A bad result can follow a sound one. This paper shows leaders how to review the outcome, the route, and the approval without confusing them.
entries.bodyHtml:
A program can hit its benefit target while bypassing controls, exhausting a key team, shifting risk, or harming customers. One green target does not describe everything the program caused.

Reviews can also make the opposite mistake. A program can miss a target after an outside event no one could reasonably predict. A bad result does not prove the approval was poor.

Ask whether the original decision was sound based only on approval-time evidence, what was achieved when the full consequence is counted, and how it was achieved compared with the approved route.

Use two grades and one attribution record. Grade the approval from its original evidence before seeing the outcome score. Then score the full outcome and compare the approved route with the route the team took.

Keep a short record at approval: the problem, alternatives, assumptions, risks, ranges, decision owner, and evidence that would reopen the choice. Keep later facts in a separate column at review.

At the next stage gate, require the record. At the next review, grade the original decision before opening the outcome score. Then score the full outcome and compare the route taken.

entries.title: Capital reallocation is the real portfolio decision
entries.summary: The annual plan records what leaders believed at the start. Portfolio governance shows what they do when the evidence changes.
entries.metaDescription: An annual plan records what you believed a year ago. Govern the portfolio by moving money and people on what you know now, in short cycles.
entries.operatingMove: Choose one scarce resource shared by two initiatives. Write the trigger, evidence, owner, and fair test period. Then run one review and record a move or hold.
entries.preview: An annual plan can lock money and people to an old view of the work. This paper shows how a short-cycle review turns new evidence into a clear choice. It uses a published trigger, a common evidence set, one decision owner, and a recorded move or hold. A fair evidence period protects useful work from churn.

entries.bodyHtml:
In the portfolios I have governed under a fixed funding ceiling, leaders often treated the annual plan as the decision. They spent months dividing money and people across initiatives. Then they defended that split until the next planning round.

The harder decision comes in month four. New evidence shows that one initiative is working, another is not, and a third now matters more. Can the portfolio move scarce capacity, or must it wait for next year's budget?

McKinsey surveyed more than 10,000 leaders and managers for its 2026 organization report. Forty-seven percent said they reviewed budget and talent only once a year or less. Only 30 percent said their organizations moved resources across the enterprise. The survey does not set one right schedule. It does show that annual review is common while enterprise-wide movement is rare.

An annual plan records what leaders believed at one point in time. When it hardens, funding stays with an initiative even after its case weakens. Scarce people stay with work that has become less valuable. Reviews then ask whether each project matches its plan, not whether it is still the best use of the next dollar or specialist.

Project status still matters. But a project can be on plan and still be the wrong place for the next unit of capacity. Portfolio governance begins when an accountable owner can compare active choices and change the allocation.

A short-cycle reallocation review can run monthly or quarterly, based on how quickly useful evidence appears. It follows a small loop: observe the evidence, compare the current use with real alternatives, move the resource or record a hold, and name what must be seen before the next review.

Four controls make that loop work: a published trigger, a small evidence set, one decision owner, and a move or recorded hold. Each initiative also needs a fair evidence period so leaders do not confuse an early wobble with a failed premise.

The unit of review is the contested resource and the real alternatives that could use it. A reallocation brief names the resource, time window, original promise, current evidence, dependencies, alternatives, and cost of doing nothing. It organizes the meeting around a choice, not a status report.

The annual plan tells leaders what they believed at the start. Reallocation shows what they do when the evidence changes.

entries.title: Choose AI limits before the model
entries.summary: Before comparing AI vendors, set the use, data, action limit, work split, and review triggers. Then choose a model that fits.
entries.metaDescription: Set provisional limits on what the AI may do and touch, before you compare vendors. Then check the vendor you picked against them before you sign.
entries.operatingMove: Take one AI request entering sourcing. Write its five limits on one page before comparing vendors.
entries.preview: A strong demo can make a vendor choice feel settled before anyone agrees on the approved use, data access, or action limit. Set those limits first, test the chosen option before commitment, and reopen the decision if they expand.
entries.bodyHtml:
A model can look impressive and still be wrong for the work, data, or actions an organization is ready to support. Before comparing vendors, state what the system may do and what it may not do.

Start with five choices: the use, data, action limit, work split, and approval triggers. Name the owner for each. Then compare models that fit those choices.

Set the first limits before the shortlist. Before commitment, test the selected model, hosting, contract, supplier chain, and workflow against them. If the candidate needs broader data or more power, return that change for a visible decision.

This is not legal advice. It gives legal, security, data, procurement, and business owners a reliable fact pattern before a vendor's defaults become the operating design.

Record the evidence, owner, date, and status for each choice. Mark it as a fact, judgment, or open question. Give every open question an owner and a due date.

New users, a new region, a different data class, an outside integration, or an automated action can all send the decision back for review.

Use one page for an AI request entering sourcing. Write the use, data, action limit, work split, and review triggers before comparing vendors.

entries.title: Who gets to decide
entries.summary: Evidence does not change work by itself. For choices that matter, name who builds the case, flags a binding constraint, decides, and changes the work.
entries.metaDescription: Name who recommends, who agrees, who decides, and who does the work. Then put those names where the work actually moves.
entries.operatingMove: Pick five recent decisions. Name who built the case, could block an option for a stated reason, decided, and changed the work.
entries.preview: A team can have the right data and still leave with no decision. This paper shows how to name who builds the case, checks a binding constraint, decides, and makes the change so evidence leads to action.
entries.bodyHtml:
A review can show that a project is late, a risk has changed, or another team needs the same people. The meeting still ends with a request for more analysis when no one has the right to redirect, pause, or stop the work.

An org chart does not answer that question. It names jobs. A decision contract names who takes each step when a real choice arrives.

First, name the recommender. That person builds the case, options, evidence, and due date. Second, name any agree role. Use a veto only for a real legal, safety, or policy limit, and require an option or an escalation path.

Third, name the decider. One person can close most operating choices. A board or required group can decide when the rules demand it, but the contract must say how the group closes the vote. Fourth, name the performer who changes the funding, work, permission, or record.

Add the four jobs to the intake form, stage gate, decision record, and delivery system. If an agree role rejects a plan, record the limit, an acceptable option, and where the case goes next. If the decider misses the due date, pause, escalate, or use a short, recorded extension.

An agent can prepare a recommendation or act inside an approved limit. Named people still set the limit, decide exceptions, and own recovery. A rule can stop an unsafe action without gaining the right to restart the work.

Use the full contract for choices that are hard to reverse, affect other teams, or create real exposure. Keep low-cost choices close to the work.

Pick five recent decisions. Trace who built the case, who could block it, who closed it, and who changed the work. Repair the missing role, rule, or workflow step before the next decision arrives.

entries.title: Standardize the Component, Not the Project
entries.summary: Do not turn a whole project into a template. Promote the smallest piece that can travel: an intake question, a readiness check, a handoff rule. Do it only after another team has used it in live work, its allowed variations are written down, and someone owns it.
entries.metaDescription: Do not turn a whole project into a template. Promote the smallest piece that travels, once another team has used it and someone owns it.
entries.operatingMove: Run a review that names the repeated piece and shows it working where it is meant to be used. Assign an owner. Publish the variations that are still valid. Define how versions change, watch the exceptions, and state what would retire it.
entries.preview: Projects mature under different sponsors, risks, technologies, contracts, and histories. Copying a whole project carries all of those local assumptions with it, and the variation comes back as rework or quiet noncompliance. The more useful move is to promote the smallest working piece: an intake question, a decision record, a readiness check, a source standard, an exception route, a measure definition, a handoff rule. It earns promotion once it has been reused and the room for local judgment is explicit. One owner can govern changes, exceptions come back as design evidence, and teams can see when it should be revised or retired. A repository supports that. It does not create organizational learning by itself.

A five-stage path from local use to a supported standard anyone can rely on

entries.bodyHtml:
A project folder is evidence, not a standard

A successful project finishes and its documents enter a shared repository. Another team copies them, changes what does not fit, and saves a second version. Soon the organization has several files with similar names, uncertain owners, and conflicting rules. The artifacts survived. The learning did not become dependable.

A PMI Global Congress paper on mature lessons-learned practice makes the missing work clear: capture is followed by analysis, retrieval, management action, and tracked follow-through. A GAO review of NASA reached the same boundary from the other direction. NASA had an agency-wide lessons system, yet the review found no assurance that lessons were being applied to later missions. Storage helps people find material. It cannot decide what the organization should rely on.

That decision belongs in the operating model. The EPMO can turn repeated project learning into a shared asset by promoting the smallest useful component, protecting the variation that context requires, and making the component’s lifecycle visible.

Promote the component that can travel

Whole projects are poor units of standardization. Their sponsors, technologies, contracts, risks, and delivery histories differ. Copying the whole project imports those local assumptions and produces a large template that teams must obey or quietly dismantle.

A reusable component is narrower. It may be an intake question that exposes whether a sponsor can name the outcome. It may be a decision record, source standard, readiness check, exception route, measure definition, or handoff rule. Each has one operating job and can be tested apart from the project that produced it.

The component needs a stable core and an explicit edge. The core states what must remain true. The edge states where local judgment begins. Kirchmer’s APQC process report supports context-driven variants alongside reference models and process governance. The standard is therefore the governed relationship between the shared core and its legitimate variants.

Promotion must be earned

A useful artifact should not become a standard because an executive likes it or one project went well. Promotion is a portfolio decision about whether another team should be able to rely on it. I use five states to manage that decision: iterate, mature, canonize, lock, and monitor.

Iterate keeps a new component close to the work while its purpose and limits are still being learned. Mature tests the core in another setting. Canonize publishes the supported core, owner, boundary, variants, and known limits. Lock places silent local edits under a visible change path. Monitor watches use, exceptions, workarounds, and obsolescence. These states are my governance framework, not an industry maturity scale or a promise of return.

Run a project-to-standard review

The review should stay small enough to make a decision at the table. Seven questions keep it honest:

Repeated component: What exact part of the work has appeared in more than one project?

Evidence of reuse: Where did another team use the core, and what changed at its intended operating point?

Owner: Who can judge the core, approve variants, publish change, and retire it?

Approved variants: What stays stable, where does local choice begin, and which differences are sanctioned?

Version path: How does a proposed change become part of the core, an approved variant, a rejection, or a request for more evidence?

Exception signal: Which repeated workaround, override, or failure forces review?

Retirement trigger: What would make the component obsolete, redundant, unsafe, or too costly to maintain?

Distribution is not evidence of reuse. Downloads and page views show exposure. The stronger evidence shows that the component entered the work at the intended point and changed a named ambiguity, handoff, or control condition. A project can attach a standard decision record while making the real choice in an unrecorded side meeting. The review must see that difference.

Variation is design data

Legitimate variation is part of the asset. PMI-sponsored innovation-governance research describes the tension between rigor and flexibility and recommends governance tailored to context. The practical answer is to give each departure a status.

An approved variant repeats under a named condition and preserves the component’s purpose. An exception permits a bounded departure for one case, with an owner and a return condition. A proposed core change shows that the shared rule no longer handles the work it was meant to govern. Variants are published, exceptions are watched for recurrence, and core changes enter the version path. Treating all three as local customization would hide the signal that improves the component.

Keep the EPMO in its lane

The EPMO governs promotion; it does not author every component or pull every local choice upward. Subject-matter owners retain authority over the content. Project leaders retain responsibility for fit. Control functions keep their existing rights.

The EPMO is positioned to scan across projects, convene the promotion decision, keep the core and approved variants visible, and aggregate exception patterns that one project cannot see. It should also resist turning every useful local practice into an enterprise obligation. Maintenance is real work, and many candidates should remain local.

A shared component earns reliance when another team can use its stable core, select a valid variant, find the current version, reach an accountable owner, report an exception, and know when the asset should retire. That is organizational learning made inspectable — without pretending that every project should look the same.

entries.title: The exception path is the real automated workflow
entries.summary: Ask a team that calls its workflow automated to show you the exception queue. It is often a shared mailbox where everything the automation could not handle quietly piles up. No owners, no classification, no record of what was tried.
entries.metaDescription: A workflow is only automated if it handles the mess. Sort the exceptions, give each kind an owner, and design the way back to normal.
entries.operatingMove: Design the exception path before you call the main path automated. Every kind of exception needs to be detected, routed to a named owner, contained, and brought back to a known state.
entries.preview: The easy path is the simplest part of a workflow to automate. It is also the least useful test of whether the operation is ready. This paper is about what happens when inputs are missing, a case is ambiguous, a dependency changes, or something falls outside the rules. Moving the routine cases to a machine means the ones left for people are, by construction, the hard ones. The paper treats the exception path as part of the automated workflow itself: detection, routing, ownership, evidence, recovery, and learning.

entries.title: The coordination tax
entries.summary: In one report-drafting workflow, drafting time per report fell from four hours to twenty minutes. The function's total output did not move. The saved hours went into picking source data, fixing formats, explaining what was generated, waiting on a new approval, and reconciling numbers against the ledger.
entries.metaDescription: Automation can cut task time while the coordination around it grows. Map the handoffs, queues, approvals, and exceptions before counting the savings.
entries.operatingMove: Before you claim a workflow is streamlined, map what happens between the tasks: the handoffs, the queues, the approvals, and who owns the exceptions. Automation that leaves that work untouched moves the cost instead of removing it.
entries.preview: Work can look efficient at the level of one task and still be slow and expensive around it. The cost sits in the handoffs, queues, approvals, and exceptions. This paper makes that cost visible. It maps the work between the tasks, and separates the coordination that earns its keep from the routing that does not. It also shows why automation that ignores ownership and recovery often shifts the burden rather than removing it.

entries.title: An AI evaluation is a production operating control
entries.summary: The workflow passed its test before launch. Then the vendor updated the model, another team changed the input format, and the work was extended to cases the test never covered. Each change was reasonable on its own, and quality slipped for weeks before a downstream complaint surfaced it.
entries.metaDescription: A launch test cannot protect a workflow whose model, inputs, and cases keep changing. Run AI evaluation as a continuing production control instead.
entries.operatingMove: Keep testing after launch. Hold a set of real cases, watch for drift, turn every incident into a new test case, and name who can narrow what the workflow is allowed to rely on.
entries.preview: A test that runs once cannot protect a workflow whose users, data, models, and consequences keep changing. This paper treats evaluation as a control you keep running: a maintained set of true-to-life cases, thresholds set by consequence, exception review, drift signals, lessons from incidents, and an owner who can change what the workflow may rely on. The launch test is usually not wrong. It is abandoned.

entries.title: Local AI versus cloud AI is a governance decision
entries.summary: Teams often argue local against cloud as if it were a technology preference. It is not. The answer falls out of seven questions about the work itself, and two workflows in the same company can land on different answers.
entries.metaDescription: Local or cloud AI is a governance decision, not a technology preference. Answer seven questions about the workflow before you name a model.
entries.operatingMove: Before anyone names a model, answer seven things for the workflow: where the data may go, who can reach the system, what it is allowed to do, how its behavior gets checked as things change, what happens when it fails, who runs it in year three, and how you leave.
entries.preview: Local or cloud is usually argued as a technology preference. This paper treats it as a governance decision instead: seven questions about the workflow itself, answered before any model is named. Where the data may go, who can reach the system, what it is allowed to do, how its behavior gets checked, what happens when it fails, who supports it, and how you leave. One camp has benchmarked the frontier cloud models and wants the best one. The other wants anything sensitive on hardware the company can touch. Both argue about models, and architecture becomes a sunk decision while they do. The paper also covers where a hybrid or a deliberately limited setup is the better answer.

entries.title: The demo-to-production gap
entries.summary: A demo shows what a system can do with inputs someone chose in advance. Production asks whether real work can depend on it in ordinary conditions, under change, and when something goes wrong.
entries.metaDescription: A demo proves what can work with chosen inputs. Production needs an owner, the messy cases, monitoring, recovery, and a way to stop it.
entries.operatingMove: Before a real workflow depends on a system that has only passed a demo, name who owns it, test it on the messy cases, put monitoring and a recovery path in place, and agree how it gets stopped and who can stop it.
entries.preview: The demo runs clean: a handful of cases picked from thousands, in the formats the system handles best, with none of the messy ones that make up a third of the real work. Nothing dishonest happens in that room. Demos exist to show what is possible. The failure comes afterward, when possibility is quietly promoted to proof and nobody asks what changed between the two worlds. This paper sets out the evidence you need before ordinary users, ordinary data, and ordinary pressure are allowed to depend on it.

entries.title: Confident and wrong
entries.summary: Fluent AI output is convincing whether or not it is right. Before anyone leans on it for a decision that matters, someone has to be able to test that confidence — and be allowed to reject the answer.
entries.metaDescription: Fluent AI output convinces whether or not it is right. A challenge protocol that tests assumptions, checks evidence, and names who can reject the answer.
entries.operatingMove: Before AI output can be relied on for a decision that matters, require four things. Name the assumptions. Check the claim against evidence from somewhere else. Write down what is still uncertain. And name the person who can stop or correct it.
entries.preview: Plausibility is one of the most useful qualities of generative AI and one of its most dangerous. This paper looks at what happens when fluent output enters a workflow with no challenge step, no independent evidence, and nobody named who can reject it. It turns “verify the output” into a real control: the questions to ask, the records to keep, the thresholds to hold, and where to escalate. entries.title: A portfolio needs scenarios, not a single annual plan
entries.summary: One annual plan stops describing reality the moment capacity, demand, or assumptions change. Keep a few workable versions of the portfolio instead. Agree in advance what you would protect, delay, reshape, or stop.
entries.metaDescription: One annual plan stops fitting the moment demand or capacity shifts. Keep a few workable portfolio scenarios instead, with agreed triggers.
entries.operatingMove: Keep a small set of workable portfolio shapes that show capacity, dependencies, and tradeoffs. Agree the triggers ahead of time. When conditions change, leaders should be choosing between options they already prepared, not improvising around a frozen plan.
entries.preview: A single annual plan gets less useful the moment capacity, dependencies, demand, or assumptions shift. Every plan eventually meets a surprise. What matters is what happens next. Most portfolios respond by keeping up appearances. Everything stays alive, delay spreads evenly, and the plan stays formally in force long after it stopped describing anything. This paper prepares the options in advance instead, with triggers and regular reviews, so leaders can move between them deliberately.

entries.summary: The post-mortem starts with the usual suspects: estimation, complexity, the vendor. Then someone walks the calendar and finds five weeks spent waiting on a policy question, a tradeoff, or an owner who was never named.
entries.metaDescription: Delay often traces to decisions nobody owns. A decision inventory records the choice, its owner, the evidence needed, and the last useful date.
entries.operatingMove: Keep a list of the choices the work is waiting on. For each one, record what has to be decided, who decides it, what evidence could change the decision, the last useful date, what stops if it slips, and what was finally decided.

It helps leaders tell a real delivery problem from a question that was simply allowed to drift.

entries.summary: A CFO asks the simplest question about the biggest investment on the page: if we stopped this today, what would we lose? The deck knows the burn rate, the milestone variance, and the issue count. It cannot answer.
entries.metaDescription: A status deck cannot say what you would lose by stopping. A PMO dashboard should show benefit, confidence, capacity, and open decisions beside spend.
entries.operatingMove: Put expected benefit, confidence, capacity pressure, unresolved decisions, and risk next to schedule and spend. A dashboard should help leaders change the portfolio, not just watch it.

Ninety minutes of review can pass without the one question that justified the meeting getting a page. This paper defines a view built for deciding: expected value, confidence, capacity pressure, unresolved choices, dependencies, and risk, set beside schedule and spend. The goal is to change the portfolio while there is still time, not to explain the outcome afterward.

entries.title: The EPMO's job is capacity, not calendars
entries.summary: Every project has a date and every plan looks solid on its own. But the same few people, systems, and approval forums turn up in all of them. Each plan is fine. The sum is fiction.
entries.metaDescription: Every plan looks sound alone while the same scarce people appear in all of them. Govern EPMO demand against real capacity, not against the calendar.
entries.operatingMove: Govern real demand against the people and systems you actually have, by role, skill, and dependency. The calendar shows what everyone intends to do. The decision is which work gets the scarce capacity and which work waits.

This paper puts the EPMO's attention on active demand and the capacity that constrains it, and gives leaders a way to expose overload, compare tradeoffs, and decide which commitments move, change shape, or wait.

entries.title: Stage gates work only when they can kill projects
entries.summary: A gate earns its place only when evidence can change the next commitment of money, people, or scope.
entries.metaDescription: A gate that cannot stop anything is a status meeting. Stage gates govern only when they carry real authority to redirect, pause, or kill a project.
entries.operatingMove: Test one mid-sized gate. Give the forum five real choices, tie evidence to the next commitment, and confirm that money and people move with the decision.
entries.preview: A gate that can only note progress is not governing the work. This paper shows how to give a review forum real authority, ask for evidence that fits the next commitment, keep five outcomes open, check key claims independently, and reopen approval when conditions change.

Pindyck, “Irreversibility, Uncertainty, and Investment,” Journal of Economic Literature 29(3), 1991, 1110–1148; NBER Working Paper 3307, 1990 — Pindyck's investment theory explains that an irreversible choice gives up the option to wait for more information; it is not a study of project reviews.
entries.bodyHtml:
Ask a portfolio board when its last review changed a project's money, people, or scope. If no one can name a case, the board may be tracking work rather than governing it. A real stage gate is a decision point. It decides whether the organization should continue, redirect, narrow, pause, or stop its next commitment to a project.

This matters because momentum gets harder to break. Leaders announce the work. Teams defend it. Contracts are signed. Early doubt becomes sunk cost, and stopping starts to feel like failure. Research on escalation of commitment shows that personal responsibility and negative framing can keep people tied to a failing course. The average sunk-cost effect is positive, though it varies across studies.

Five properties give a gate teeth

First, the forum needs written authority to act. Its charter should say what it may decide, what still belongs to a sponsor or executive committee, and how conflicts move upward. A condition is real only if funding, staffing, scope, or reliance changes when the forum sets it.

Second, the evidence should fit the next commitment. A short, reversible test needs less proof than a large spend or a dependency that other programs will build around. Start with the decision, then name the few facts that must be true. Put those facts on a one-page evidence map with the test, result, owner, and open question.

Third, all five outcomes must work in practice: continue, redirect, narrow, pause, and stop. Define what happens to people, money, and unfinished work after each choice. Otherwise, every choice except continue becomes a new negotiation, and the board will keep weak work moving because that path is easiest.

Fourth, advocates should not be the only owners of key evidence. A sponsor may argue for the project. Finance can still check the benefit math, operations can test whether the change can be absorbed, and architecture can review the integration claim. This is not a claim of bad faith. It is a way to keep hope from becoming the only forecast.

Fifth, approval conditions need a trigger and an end date. If a key supplier slips, adoption falls, or the cost rises past an agreed point, the decision returns to the forum. An old approval should not become permanent permission for work that has changed.

Test one gate before changing the whole process

Choose one mid-sized decision with real stakes. Replace the standing checklist with a one-page evidence map. Write down the five possible outcomes before the meeting. Record the choice, conditions, dissent, owner, and expiry date in the room. Then confirm that money and people moved as directed.

After two or three reviews, ask a blunt question: What changed because this gate met? If the answer is still nothing material, fix the authority before adding more templates. A gate earns its place when evidence can change the next commitment while the organization still has options.

entries.title: A project is not ready because a plan exists
entries.summary: A finished plan is not readiness. Before more money and people go in, four things have to be true: someone can make the first hard decisions, the outcome and its limits are written down, the people you need have agreed dates, and the capacity is named.
entries.metaDescription: A finished plan is not readiness. Confirm four things first: who decides, what the outcome is, who takes part, and who is free to do the work.
entries.operatingMove: Before kickoff, confirm in writing who can make the first hard decisions. Name one business outcome you can test, and say what this stage will not attempt. Turn the stakeholder list into dated commitments from their managers. Then name the people and the hours. A filled-in plan is not proof that the project is ready.

This paper treats readiness as something earned before the next commitment, not a checklist attached to a date. It gives sponsors and delivery leaders a proportionate way to narrow, stage, delay, or approve the work based on what is actually known.

entries.title: The prove-it economy is coming for careers and AI programs
entries.summary: A working demonstration and a credible leadership story can still leave a sponsor unable to inspect the claim. One record built during the work can carry two things: the next AI investment decision, and the leader's later account of their own part in it.
entries.metaDescription: A demo and a good story can still leave a sponsor unable to inspect the claim. One evidence record built during delivery can serve both reviews.
entries.operatingMove: Before the next review that matters, pick one claim the decision rests on. Write down six things: the claim, the context and the work, the evidence, the result or what was learned, the limits, and who owns it and what they decide next. Narrow or delay any claim the record cannot support.
entries.preview: The sponsor's question survives the demonstration. What shows that this works under normal conditions, within known limits, with someone accountable for it? This field note follows that gap into later scrutiny by people and by machines. It rejects the idea of building two proof packs late. Instead one record, built claim by claim during the work, serves two different decisions without overstating either.
entries.bodyHtml:
The sponsor's question survives the demonstration

You lead an enterprise AI program and are preparing the case for its next funding decision. The demonstration works. The team can explain the workflow and intended benefit. Then the sponsor asks: What can we inspect? Does the program work outside the demonstration, within known limits, under accountable ownership?

A demonstration shows capability under selected conditions. It cannot reconstruct what happened in normal use. The sponsor needs a record for a high-stakes decision. That record must show the result, the conditions that shaped it, the known limits, the response to failure, and the owner of the next decision.

What the evidence record has to cover

AI-service FactSheets, the NIST Generative AI Profile, and the GAO accountability framework approach the problem from different directions. They point to service disclosures, monitoring, incident response, and accountable governance. These are useful categories for a record. The sources do not show that every buyer or board has adopted one standard.

That boundary matters. The record should support the exact claim under review. A source can sit beside a sentence it does not support. An artifact can look rigorous while proving little. The evaluator still has to check the evidence and its limits.

Why the missing record follows the leader

The sponsor can ask the team for evidence directly. A later evaluator may encounter only what a search or answer system can retrieve. Research on generative engine optimization tested part of that process. On its benchmark, citations, credible quotations, and statistics improved a source's visibility in generated answers. The result applies to that benchmark. It shows why evidence-bearing text gives a generative system material to use.

The finding does not predict an individual's hiring outcome. It identifies a practical disadvantage for an accurate claim that is poorly documented: neither a person nor a system can inspect evidence that was never retained.

The apparent duplication

The program team can assemble a board pack when approval is due. Months later, the leader can rebuild a career story from memory and whatever artifacts remain. Separate preparation can seem reasonable. A board decides whether to fund or stop. A career reader assesses the leader's judgment and contribution.

The better operating choice is one record created during delivery. The board review and the later career claim can both draw from it. The two presentations remain distinct. Evidence made during the work supports the program decision. Later use stays bounded to the leader's contribution and confidentiality obligations.

Build the record around one claim

Before the next major review, choose one claim the decision depends on. Record six things: the exact claim; the context and work; the evidence produced; the result or learning; the limits; and the owner, refresh trigger, and next decision. Keep the evidence near the claim so another person can inspect it without rebuilding the story.

Match the standard to the decision. Low-stakes work in a trusted relationship may need little formal proof. The record earns its cost when the impact justifies checking. It also helps when the evaluator is unfamiliar with the claimant or a machine mediates the assessment.

Keep the career use bounded

LinkedIn's recruiting research supports attention to skills assessment. It does not measure whether a public portfolio changes an individual's hiring outcome. Treat the resume as an index to defensible claims. Confidential evidence can remain private, anonymized, aggregated, or described through a method. Retain only what the career claim needs and what confidentiality permits.

Return to the program review. If the six-field record cannot support the claim, narrow the claim or delay the decision until the missing evidence exists. Build the record while its context can still be checked. Later career use then adapts retained evidence instead of rebuilding a story from memory.

entries.bodyHtml:
You are told to add more AI agents, find more uses, and get more work done. The plan may count model cost and technical skill. It may not ask a harder question: How many AI decisions can your people still review, explain, and stand behind?

Every agent adds output. It also adds work for people who check important results, handle exceptions, and answer when the system is wrong. If agents grow faster than that human work, the company gains output it cannot fully own.

McKinsey expects human oversight to limit how widely companies can use AI agents. It also reports that teams of two to five people can already supervise 50 to 100 specialized agents. That is an early figure, not a safe benchmark for every company. It still points to the question leaders need to answer: Where is the limit for this team and this work?

Put a number on supervision

The span of supervision is how many agents or units of AI work one accountable person can genuinely own. The span gets smaller when errors are costly, hard to see, or hard to reverse. It can be larger when errors are easy to spot and fix.

Use a weekly test. Can the named owner explain what the agent did, what was checked, what failed, and what changed? If the honest answer is no, the team has already taken on more than it can supervise.

Review by risk

Oversight does not mean reading every output. Low-risk work may need sampling. High-risk work may need a person to approve each case. New or uncertain work may need tighter review until the team knows its failure patterns. Write down what is sampled, what always gets checked, what triggers a deeper review, and who can stop the workflow.

Use tools, but keep a human owner

Critic agents, guardrails, monitoring, tests, and incident response can help a small team supervise more work. They can find common errors and send unusual cases to people. They still need their own tests and monitoring. A named person must be able to change or stop them.

Treat review time as shared capacity

Every live AI system draws on a shared group of reviewers and experts. Each funding request should name the owner, expected review load, type of review, experts needed for hard cases, and conditions that would pause or stop the work. When that pool is full, move attention away from stable, low-risk work before adding more demand.

Start with one workflow

Track the owner's review and follow-up time for four weeks. Check whether exceptions reached the right person and whether the owner can explain what changed. Use that evidence to adjust the span before another agent goes live. AI can grow only as fast as the organization can still answer for what it does.

entries.bodyHtml:
Most AI tools can report active users, sessions, and feature use within days. Those numbers answer a useful question: Did people open the tool? They do not answer the question leaders funded the program to solve: Did recurring work get faster, better, or less costly?

In a Gartner survey, 49 percent of respondents named estimating and showing AI value as the main barrier to adoption. A preliminary MIT NANDA study, reported by Fortune, found little or no measurable profit-and-loss effect for most pilots in its dataset. The study was preliminary and the report was secondary, so the figure is a warning, not a universal failure rate.

Measure the workflow in three layers

First, check whether AI reached the people and tasks in the target workflow. Tool-use data shows breadth and concentration. It does not show value by itself.

Second, check whether the workflow result moved. Use records the operation already keeps: cycle time, throughput, errors, rework, escalations, approval time, or another result leaders already care about. Pair speed or volume with quality so a visible gain does not hide later work.

Third, test whether AI is a credible reason for the change. Compare the workflow before and after, compare similar teams, sample quality, or check a manager's account against the records. State what the comparison can and cannot support.

Set the rules before seeing the answer

Name the workflow owner, data owner, and AI program owner. Write the baseline and follow-up periods, the measures, the comparison method, the level of tool use needed for a fair test, and the people who must confirm the result.

End with a choice

Every review should end with one of four choices: continue, hold, change, or stop. Record the choice, owner, reason, next check, and any condition that would reopen it.

Measure without watching every person

Use the least personal data that can answer the workflow question. Avoid keystroke logs, screen recordings, and a record of every prompt. Tell people what is measured, why it matters, who can see it, and which decision it supports.

Start with one recurring workflow

Choose one workflow with enough volume to measure. Ask: Which result changed, by how much, against what baseline, and with what evidence that AI contributed? If the program cannot answer, it may still be a useful experiment. It is not yet proof that the operation improved.

entries.title: Every agent needs a human operating model
entries.summary: A capable agent clears its pilot, and the decision to switch it on lands with one leader who will answer for everything it does next. What has to be true before it is allowed to touch real work?

Make that completed canvas the gate an agent has to clear before it is funded.

entries.bodyHtml:
A capable agent clears its pilot. The decision to put it into production lands on one leader's desk. The demo was clean and the model is genuinely capable. Approving it means handing the agent a license, a live workflow, and real customers and real data to act on. At that moment there is no settled answer to a plain question. The agent makes a judgment call, escalates the wrong case, or returns an output that looks finished and is wrong. Who in the organization owns that result?

The gap is not hypothetical. Gartner projects that more than 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. The reasons it cites are rising costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls. Gartner does name immature models. But its headline reasons point past the model to how agents are chosen and governed.

The Agent Operating-Model Canvas

My claim is narrow and testable. An agent belongs in production only after a named human can answer seven things about it.

1. Role and scope

What is it for, and where does it stop? Scope creep is how agents end up making decisions nobody designed them to make.

2. What it may decide, and what it may not

What may it decide alone, what needs a sign-off, what must go up the line? Left unwritten, authority defaults to the widest reading anyone can give it.

3. How it escalates and stops

A path for cases it should not handle, and a halt that exists before it is needed. One bad assumption at speed becomes a thousand bad outputs.

4. What has to challenge it

Before anyone trusts an output, what had to disagree with it and be overruled? Confident wrong answers are the expensive ones.

5. What a good result looks like

Define good before the agent produces anything. Otherwise review collapses into a check for plausibility, which is the check a fluent model defeats best.

6. What evidence it leaves

A trail that lets a human work out what it did and why. That is what turns standards like NIST's into daily practice.

7. Who owns the result

One named person who owns the outcomes. Not a committee. Not the vendor. If no name attaches, it does not ship.

The real ceiling

The canvas reads like a checklist you fill in once per agent. That invites an obvious next move: fill it in again and keep adding agents. But the seventh element breaks that plan. Every agent needs one named human owner, and no human can answer for an unlimited number. So the canvas that governs one agent also caps how many you can run.

Human oversight is finite, and it runs out before model capability does. McKinsey reports that teams of two to five people can already supervise 50 to 100 agents. It also expects how far agents spread to be capped by how much oversight people can provide. Add agents without adding oversight and you do not grow output. You grow exposure. So fund the oversight as a standing cost, and make a completed canvas the gate an agent has to clear before it is funded.

What to do next

Before your next agent goes live, apply the simplest version of the test. Name the person who would stand up in a review and account for its decisions. If that name does not exist, or is really a group that adds up to no one, the deployment is premature, however capable the model is.

The white paper works through all seven canvas elements and the failure each one prevents. It adds a symptom-to-gap table for reading trouble back to its missing element, three governed agents from portfolio work, and the funding-gate move that keeps the count of live agents tied to the people available to answer for them.

entries.title: Enterprise AI trust is built through operating evidence, not tool novelty
entries.summary: A capable AI pilot can impress everyone and still stall before it reaches important work. A better model will not move it if the people accountable for its use still lack proof they can rely on it. That proof supports judgment; it does not certify the system.
entries.operatingMove: Choose the AI use that would cause the most harm if it were wrong. Build one current evidence pack with a named owner for that use. Show what the system did, the basis for its result, its tested limits, and who answers for relying on it. The pack does not certify the system or replace judgment; it supports the owner's decision to rely, retest, or hold back.
entries.preview: A strong AI pilot stalls before it reaches the core workflow that would justify the investment. Asking for a better model misreads the problem. This field note shows the four questions a named owner must answer before the business can rely on the system. A current evidence pack supports that judgment; it does not certify the system.
entries.bodyHtml:
A capable AI pilot impresses everyone in the demo. It gets a funded trial and then stalls. The system stays on low-stakes tasks at the edge of the business. It never enters the work that would justify the investment. The usual response is to ask for a better model.

That response misreads the problem. Model quality is not always the missing piece. The organization is holding the system outside important work because accountable leaders cannot answer one question: can we rely on it? Novelty does not answer that question.

I see this pattern in governance work. Programs offer usage dashboards and demo decks as proof. Usage only shows that people tried the tool. Reliance needs evidence that the tool did the right thing, on a sound basis, within known limits, under a named owner.

What a business checks before it relies on a system

Trust becomes governable when a named owner can prove it on demand. For a given use, the owner must show four things: what the system did, the basis for its result, where it has and has not been tested, and who answers for relying on it. If one is missing, the system is not yet trustworthy for that use. The evidence, not the demo, supports the decision.

The evidence pack

That proof travels with the system as an evidence pack. The pack states the purpose and intended use. It records test results and conditions, safety and security, data and model sources, tested limits, human review, and the named owner. AI FactSheets offer a research model for the record. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework gives teams a loop to keep the system under review as its use changes.

Evidence builds value as it travels. A system that earned trust in one workflow arrives at the next with its proof attached. The owner can review what changed instead of starting the whole trust debate again.

Keeping the evidence current

A pack filed once is only a snapshot. Models drift, inputs change, and use can move beyond what was tested. The named owner keeps the pack current and repeats tests as use grows. This also helps the team move faster. It can extend a trusted system into new work without starting from zero.

Where evidence discipline goes wrong

Evidence can fail in three common ways. Evidence theater counts activity but does not prove reliable results. False precision uses a number that implies more testing than the team performed. An approval-only pack clears a gate and then goes stale as the system changes. Each creates the look of evidence without doing its job. The test is whether the named owner can still answer for the system today.

The pack is not a certification or a substitute for judgment. It gives the named owner evidence to decide whether to rely, retest, or hold back.

Start with one high-consequence use

Do not try to earn trust across the whole AI portfolio at once. Choose the use that would cause the most harm if it were wrong. Build one current evidence pack with a named owner for that use. Make it easy to inspect. That first pack becomes the model for the next team. A better model will not move the pilot parked at the edge. Evidence will.

entries.title: The write-up you skipped never gets blamed
entries.summary: When a meeting ends and nobody writes down what was decided, the next team has to stop and ask or start and guess. The hour you saved comes back in their queue, logged as a clarification, a redesign, or a reopened decision. What it never gets logged as is the write-up nobody did.

entries.bodyHtml:
Your steering group approved a change. The next team is ready to start. The schedule is already slipping, so someone makes a sensible-sounding offer: begin the handoff now, write up the decision later. It sounds fine, because everyone in the meeting already knows what happened. The next team does not.

They need to know what changed, why it changed, what you agreed to bend, and who is allowed to change it again. Without that, the person picking up the work has two choices: stop and ask, or start and guess. Both put more pressure on the schedule you were trying to protect.

So does starting sooner actually save time, once the decision has to cross into someone else's work? The answer shows up in what happens after the meeting.

Where the time actually goes

Writing it up is easy to skip because the cost is visible and immediate — an hour, right now, while the schedule slips. Starting the handoff is immediate too. The write-up looks like a separate job you can do any time.

Then a product team gets the scope change and comes back asking why. Operations designs the standard path and then finds out an exception was already agreed. A new manager reopens a settled decision because nobody wrote down what would have to change for it to be revisited.

Each of those gets logged as something else — a clarification, a redesign, a reopened decision. The original choice to skip the write-up never appears in the account of the delay. That is why it never gets fixed: nothing in the record points back to it.

Let the next team decide when it is done

Records matter most at the seams — a decision moving from a steering group to delivery, a design moving between functions, a program moving into operations, one owner handing off to the next. This is where knowledge has to move from the people who have it to people who do not, and survive in a form those people can use.

Length and polish prove nothing. Hand the record to the person receiving the work and ask them to trace the action they are supposed to take back to the decision, the reason behind it, where it stops applying, and who can change it. If they have to come back to you for another meeting, that gap is what the handoff is still missing.

A record that passes does four jobs. It lets the next team act. It keeps the decision and the reasoning together. It stays useful after people leave. And it gives a person, or an AI system, something reliable to look up later. All four depend on the record working without its author standing next to it.

AI cannot tell you what the page left out

A retrieval system can only find what the page actually contains. A missing reason, a missing exception, a missing owner, a missing date — none of that can be recovered from a page that never captured it. Research on retrieval systems finds that problems starting at the source carry through to the answer, and NIST lists where data came from and how good it is among the things organizations should write down. Neither tells a retrieval system who keeps the page current. Only the page can do that.

A colleague who hits an incomplete page knows who to call. A retrieval system sees the page, whatever is attached to it, and nothing else. A better model cannot supply context that was never written down — though bad documentation is only one of the things that can make an AI answer wrong.

Give the next team five things

At the next handoff that matters, require a short record with a name on it that answers five questions. What did we decide, and what is it meant to achieve? Why did we pick it? What did we agree to bend or leave open, and what cannot change? What happens next, and who owns it? What date or event should bring this back up?

The person who made the decision stays responsible for the content even if someone else writes the words. They confirm the reasoning, the limits, and when to revisit. The person receiving it confirms they can actually use it.

Ownership does not end at acceptance. A record people rely on turns dangerous when conditions change underneath it, so someone has to be able to fix it, retire it, or flag the part where someone now has to decide for themselves. A policy change, a system change, an exception, a new decision, or a review date is what should trigger that.

Back to the handoff you were about to rush. If the record passes the next team's test, they can start without guessing, and someone is on the hook for keeping it accurate. If it fails, you know exactly what to do — fill in what is missing before you hand it over. The schedule will still be urgent. What changes is when you call it done: not when the meeting ends, but when the person receiving the work can use what you wrote.

entries.title: Business imagination is the scarce asset now
entries.summary: A portfolio review can see several promising AI proposals and still lack a sound basis for choosing which ones deserve scarce capacity.
entries.operatingMove: Before funding an AI tool, require one brief. Name the workflow or decision to change, the stakes, the evidence, the owner, the choices people still make, and the best route.
entries.preview: Cheap AI execution produces more plausible ideas than a portfolio can frame and compare. This field note shows how one opportunity brief helps. It turns an operating problem into a choice you can test before the team commits time and money.
inside: Why more output, more usage, and local wins still do not settle the portfolio decision
What one opportunity brief has to name before any tool is funded
How comparing routes and reading pilot evidence leads to one defined next step
entries.bodyHtml:
You chair the portfolio review that decides which AI ideas receive scarce capacity. One team brings a working assistant. Another has a vendor demo. A third shows time saved on drafting and analysis. All three can produce something. None has shown which work should change, what result would matter, or why AI is the right investment.

Cheaper execution is useful. Models can draft, summarize, classify, compare, search, and code. A field study of customer-support agents found a 14 percent average productivity gain in one defined workflow. Novice and lower-skilled workers gained the most. At enterprise level, McKinsey reported broad AI use but much less reported impact on earnings. A defined task can improve while a portfolio still lacks a sound way to choose among investments.

That gap has a cost. Capacity can follow the polished prototype, the familiar vendor, or the metric that is easiest to count. A promising operating problem may stay hidden because no one has framed it as a choice. Another team may carry a demo forward without showing which business result it can change.

The first constraint is the judgment to frame the work

A portfolio needs evidence about the work and its result. Counts of users, prompts, documents, code suggestions, and pilots may all rise. Cycle time, quality, customer experience, risk, and financial results may not move. McKinsey separates five layers of evidence: technical performance, user adoption, operating results, strategic outcomes, and financial impact. No single activity count proves the full case.

Failure can start before a pilot. Gartner predicted in 2024 that at least 30 percent of generative AI projects would be dropped after proof of concept by the end of 2025. It cited poor data, weak risk controls, rising costs, and unclear business value. RAND interviewed 65 experienced practitioners. They most often pointed to confusion or poor communication about a project's intent and purpose as the reason AI projects failed. RAND advised leaders to focus on the problem before the technology.

Cheap execution creates more ideas than a review can frame and compare. The first limit is often the judgment needed to turn one operating problem into a testable choice. This paper calls that judgment business imagination. It is the practical skill of turning an operating problem into a choice that a portfolio can compare, test, and fund.

Put one opportunity brief before the tool decision

Require one short opportunity brief before a material AI idea receives funding or scarce delivery capacity. Use it as well before the result becomes part of recurring work. The brief names the work, what happens now, how value may appear, what evidence earns more investment, who owns the result, which decisions stay with people, and which other routes the team should compare.

Consider a proposal to improve portfolio reporting with AI. That phrase is too loose to fund. The brief may reveal a narrower problem. Analysts spend hours fixing inconsistent fields before an executive review. The late work delays the decision. The team expects a shorter preparation cycle and a more reliable report. It should compare better data checks and a fixed rule before it proposes a model.

Compare routes before committing to a tool

Model access is only one route. A short test with a leading model may fit a valuable question with an uncertain answer. Stable, repeated, low-risk work may fit a cheaper model or fixed-rule automation. Poor source data may need repair first. A high-stakes judgment may need a human expert. A weak idea should wait or stop. The review weighs value, uncertainty, risk, repeatability, and the strength of the evidence.

Connect the pilot to the business result

Keep the brief with the idea after approval. Test five links. Did the system work well enough? Did people use it in the workflow? Did the starting measure move? Did that change matter to the business? Did the result justify the full cost and risk? Early signs can stay visible without becoming a financial claim too soon.

At the next review, bring back the same brief with the evidence filled in. The portfolio can then explore, redirect, fund the next defined step, fold the idea into existing work, wait, or stop. Before funding the tool, require the team to name the work, value, evidence, owner, human judgment, and route that fit the job.

entries.title: Benefits realization is where transformations quietly fail
entries.summary: The program ships without missing a deadline anyone notices. The milestones are checked, the team is thanked, everyone moves on. Months later the value that justified the whole thing has not appeared, and nobody is sure anyone is still measuring.
entries.metaDescription: Programs ship on schedule and the value never arrives. Benefits realization needs a named owner, an agreed baseline, and a review gate after go-live.
entries.operatingMove: Name someone who owns the benefit, agree the baseline before you start, and book the realization gate at approval rather than arranging it after go-live. A project is not finished when the output ships. It is finished when you can show the operating change.
entries.preview: Most transformation failures are not dramatic. The program does not collapse or miss its deadline in a way anyone notices inside the company. It ships, and the value quietly never arrives. This paper explains how benefits lose their owner somewhere between approval, build, adoption, and everyday operation, and sets out a practical discipline: a named benefits owner, a credible baseline, early and late evidence, and a review that can change the approach when the promised result does not appear.

entries.title: The AI value test: automate, build, buy, hire, or wait
entries.summary: AI proposals usually get compared against doing nothing. Compare them against the real options instead: automate it, build it, buy it, hire for it, or wait.
entries.operatingMove: Judge automation, building, buying, hiring, and waiting against the same questions: what it is worth, what it risks, what capacity it needs, and how easily you could undo it. Do that before treating AI as the default answer.
entries.preview: AI proposals are often weighed against doing nothing, rather than against everything else you could do instead. This paper puts all five options on the same page: automate, build, buy, hire, or wait. Each is compared on how it creates value, what it costs to run, how long it takes to produce evidence, how easily it can be undone, what it depends on, and what it risks. The aim is to pick the smallest credible move without mistaking novelty for fit.
